meta.note: Computational and literature summary only. No discovery claims; not medical advice.
meta.overlooked_rule: Flagged: independent statistical genetic evidence (exome-wide or FDR rare-variant association, or a structural variant) and at most 60 PubMed title/abstract records for the official symbol, symbol not ambiguous. Since version 2.1 a database link alone (OMIM, Orphanet, ClinGen) cannot set the flag; such genes are marked 'few papers, database link only' until checked by hand. Counts use the official symbol; an alias-aware count (former names and aliases, may include homonyms) is added by the daily job. A flag is a starting point, not a finding.

mpfc.name: Medial prefrontal cortex
mpfc.does: Front, inner surface of the frontal lobe. Involved in thinking about oneself, other people and decisions.
mpfc.self: Part of the cortical midline structures that light up whenever people judge things in relation to themselves. A meta-analysis splits it into a ventral part (tagging information as 'about me') and a dorsal part (evaluating it).

acc.name: Anterior cingulate cortex
acc.does: A belt of cortex above the corpus callosum that monitors conflict and errors and links emotion to action.
acc.self: In a small PET study, people with schizophrenia who felt their movements were controlled from outside showed over-activity here and in parietal cortex; it settled as the symptom improved.

pcc.name: Posterior cingulate & precuneus
pcc.does: Inner back surface of the brain; a hub of the brain's resting 'default mode' network.
pcc.self: The posterior part of the cortical midline structures, active during self-related processing across tasks.

thal.name: Thalamus
thal.does: Central relay that passes sensory and motor signals to the cortex.
thal.self: Cortical midline structures are densely linked with subcortical midline regions; the meta-analysis argues for one cortical-subcortical midline system for the self.

hippo.name: Hippocampus & entorhinal cortex
hippo.does: Inner temporal lobe; essential for forming new memories.
hippo.self: Not covered by the self-processing sources reviewed here.

sn.name: Substantia nigra & striatum
sn.does: Dopamine-making neurons in the midbrain (substantia nigra) that signal to the striatum to start and smooth movement.
sn.self: Not covered by the self-processing sources reviewed here. Dopamine's role in the comparator model of delusions of control is named as an open question.

cereb.name: Cerebellum
cereb.does: Back of the brain under the cortex; fine-tunes movement by predicting its outcome.
cereb.self: Not covered by the self-processing sources reviewed here.

brainstem.name: Brainstem
brainstem.does: Connects brain and spinal cord; controls breathing, eye movements and arousal.
brainstem.self: An eye-movement pathway from the brainstem to the frontal cortex is the best-worked-out example of a corollary discharge, the brain's internal copy of its own movement commands; this signal appears disrupted in schizophrenia.

pfc.name: Lateral prefrontal cortex
pfc.does: Outer front of the brain; planning, working memory and control of attention.
pfc.self: Rare damaging variants in schizophrenia are most enriched in genes specific to frontal cortex (SCHEMA). Frontal brain stimulation improved action-outcome monitoring in a schizophrenia study.

motor.name: Motor & premotor cortex
motor.does: Strip in front of the central sulcus that plans and sends movement commands.
motor.self: Every movement command is sent out with a copy (corollary discharge) that lets the brain predict what it will feel. If the prediction fails, one's own actions can feel caused by someone else: the comparator model of delusions of control.

parietal.name: Inferior parietal cortex / temporo-parietal junction
parietal.does: Outer back-middle of the brain; combines body position, attention and the sense of who caused an action.
parietal.self: In patients with passivity experiences (feeling controlled from outside), this area was over-active during voluntary movement and calmed as symptoms improved (small PET study, 7 patients). Parietal cortex is a recurring candidate in self-monitoring models.

auditory.name: Auditory cortex (temporal lobe)
auditory.does: Upper temporal lobe; processes sound and speech.
auditory.self: Before we speak, motor areas warn the auditory cortex to expect our own voice. Failure of this warning is a leading explanation for why inner speech can be heard as an outside voice.

insula.name: Insula
insula.does: Cortex folded deep inside the lateral sulcus; senses the body's inner state.
insula.self: Not covered by the self-processing sources reviewed here, although it is often discussed in bodily-self research.

self_story.t: Self-disorders (from the German Ichstörungen) are changes in the first-person sense of being oneself: thoughts that feel inserted, actions that feel controlled from outside, a self that feels thin or unreal. They have long been tied to schizophrenia, especially early on.

self_story.h: How strong is the evidence that they mark schizophrenia?
self_story.t: Across 25 studies (690 patients), people with schizophrenia showed clear disturbances of the minimal self (overall effect size 0.51; sense of agency 0.49). An updated 2026 meta-analysis of 38 studies found self-disorder scores highest in the schizophrenia spectrum, intermediate in people at clinical high risk, and lower in other mental disorders. Body ownership, by contrast, was not impaired in a dedicated experiment plus meta-analysis. Agency findings also depend on the task: some studies show too little self-attribution, others too much.

self_story.h: Is there a 'centre of the I' in the brain?
self_story.t: No single centre has been found. Two systems keep coming up. (1) Cortical midline structures (medial prefrontal, anterior and posterior cingulate, precuneus) are active whenever we process information about ourselves. (2) A prediction system: each action is sent out with an internal copy (corollary discharge) so the brain can recognise the result as self-made. When this fails, one's own thoughts, speech or movements can feel foreign. Taking a first-person perspective engages medial prefrontal, medial parietal and lateral temporoparietal cortex.

Patients whose own hand acts against their will (alien limb, 50 lesion cases) had lesions in many places, but all fell within one network connected to the precuneus; lesions removing the will to act (akinetic mutism, 28 cases) mapped to a network connected to the anterior cingulate. A 2026 case analysis with systematic review of post-stroke alien hand found that the sense of agency was always disrupted, while the sense of owning the limb was lost mainly with parietal lesions.

self_story.h: Which areas look different in people with these experiences?
self_story.t: Evidence is small but specific. In a PET study, patients who felt their movements were controlled from outside over-activated parietal and cingulate cortex, and this reversed as the symptom faded. Corollary discharge deficits have been measured in speech-to-hearing and eye-movement pathways.

self_story.h: Which genes and proteins are involved?
self_story.t: No gene has been linked specifically to self-disorders: we found no study tying a risk gene to these experiences. The closest genetic bridge: people with a 22q11.2 deletion, a high-risk genetic form of schizophrenia, showed clear deficits in monitoring their own actions and over-attributed actions to themselves in virtual-reality tests, before any psychosis. This links a risk deletion to a sense-of-agency measure, not to a single gene. What is known is for schizophrenia as a whole: 287 common-variant loci concentrated in neuron-expressed genes, 10 genes with rare damaging variants of large effect (including the glutamate receptors GRIN2A and GRIA3), enrichment in frontal-cortex-specific genes, and complement C4A, which tags synapses for removal. Linking these genes to the self-network regions is an open analysis, listed as a NeuroUnknown next step.

self_story.h: Do current treatments target the cause?
self_story.t: No. All long-established antipsychotics block dopamine D2 receptors; they reduce psychosis but do not repair the underlying biology. Only about 1 in 7 people meet strict recovery criteria (median 13.5% across 50 studies), and this has not improved over decades. The first approved drug without direct D2 blockade, xanomeline-trospium (a muscarinic M1/M4 agonist), reduced symptoms in phase 3, but it also treats symptoms. A glycine-transporter drug for the glutamate hypothesis (iclepertin) failed to improve cognition in three phase 3 trials.

Not today. Many people improve and some recover, but no treatment removes the cause, because the cause is spread over hundreds of genes and developmental factors. Neurology shows what a cure-like treatment can look like when one gene is the cause: in spinal muscular atrophy, an RNA drug that corrects the faulty gene's product let 51% of treated infants reach motor milestones versus 0% without it. Schizophrenia has no single causal gene of that kind, but rare large-effect genes such as GRIN2A are the closest starting points.

self_story.h: An experimental lead on the self itself
self_story.t: A small study found that frontal transcranial direct current stimulation improved action-outcome monitoring in schizophrenia spectrum disorder, the process thought to fail in passivity experiences. This is a proof of concept, not a treatment.

diseases.name: Schizophrenia & psychosis
diseases.intro: Schizophrenia is a disorder in which perception, thinking and the sense of being oneself can change, usually beginning in late adolescence or early adulthood. It is highly heritable, but the risk is spread over hundreds of genetic variants that mostly act in neurons and synapses, together with environmental factors. Psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions are linked to disturbed signalling in dopamine and glutamate circuits; current medicines act on these signals rather than on the underlying causes.

Higher C4A complement activity raises risk; in mice C4 drives removal of synapses during development.

Of 170 environmental and developmental factors studied in 683 studies, only the ultra-high-risk clinical state and Black-Caribbean ethnicity in England had convincing evidence; urbanicity, migration, childhood trauma and childhood social withdrawal had weaker (suggestive) evidence.

diseases.name: Parkinson's disease
diseases.intro: Parkinson's disease is a progressive disorder in which dopamine-producing neurons of the substantia nigra are lost and the protein alpha-synuclein aggregates in nerve cells. It causes slowness, rigidity and tremor, and many non-motor symptoms. Dopamine replacement works well for movement symptoms but does not stop the disease.
causes: 90 independent risk signals in 37,688 cases; risk loci are brain-enriched and point to specific neuron types.
Aggregated alpha-synuclein is central to the disease process and can be detected with seed amplification assays.

diseases.name: ALS (motor neuron disease)
diseases.intro: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis destroys the motor neurons of the brain and spinal cord, causing progressive weakness. About one in 350 people develop it. Some cases are caused by single genes such as SOD1, which now allows gene-targeted treatment for that form.
causes: Lifetime risk about 1 in 350; 15 risk loci in 29,612 patients with distinct genetic architectures.
Mutations in SOD1 cause one inherited form; lowering SOD1 is a direct, cause-targeted strategy.
guidelines: EAN guideline on the management of ALS (2024)
treat: Multidisciplinary care, nutrition and ventilation support
Recommended in the EAN 2024 guideline alongside available disease-modifying treatments.
Lowered SOD1 and neurofilament; missed the 28-week primary endpoint; longer data favoured early start.
diseases.cure: Not curable. Gene-targeted silencing now exists for the SOD1 form.

diseases.name: Multiple sclerosis
diseases.intro: Multiple sclerosis is an immune-mediated disease in which inflammation damages myelin and nerve fibres in the brain, optic nerves and spinal cord. Diagnosis rests on lesions spread in space and in time, shown clinically or on MRI; oligoclonal bands in the spinal fluid can substitute for spread in time.
causes: Immune attack on myelin in the central nervous system, influenced by genetic and environmental factors.
related: Neuromyelitis optica and MOG antibody disease
other inflammatory diseases that must be distinguished from MS
diseases.cure: Not curable; disease-modifying drugs reduce relapses and new lesions.

pathway.txt: Lesions spread in space and time on MRI or clinically; spinal fluid oligoclonal bands can substitute for spread in time.

Start a disease-modifying drug approved by the EMA, chosen with the person according to disease activity, safety and pregnancy plans; monitor response with MRI and switch if the response is not good enough.
A short course of high-dose corticosteroids speeds recovery from a relapse but does not change the long-term course.

diseases.name: Ischaemic stroke
diseases.intro: In ischaemic stroke a blocked artery cuts off blood to part of the brain, and brain tissue dies within minutes to hours. The earlier blood flow is restored, the better the outcome.
causes: Blockage of a brain artery by a clot from the heart or a large artery, or by small-vessel disease.
related: bleeding into the brain; it must be excluded with imaging before clot-dissolving treatment
guidelines: AHA/ASA guideline for early management of acute ischaemic stroke (2019)
diseases.cure: Time-critical: early clot removal or dissolution reduces disability; damaged tissue does not regrow.

pathway.txt: Urgent brain imaging to exclude bleeding and to find a blocked large artery.

pathway.txt: Intravenous thrombolysis (alteplase): more benefit the earlier it is given, at the cost of a small risk of brain bleeding.

pathway.txt: Mechanical thrombectomy: in five trials it reduced disability (number needed to treat 2.6).

diseases.name: Epilepsy
diseases.intro: Epilepsy is a tendency to recurrent seizures caused by abnormal, synchronised electrical activity of neurons. Seizures are classified as focal (starting in one network of one hemisphere) or generalised (engaging both hemispheres from the start).
causes: Causes include structural lesions (for example hippocampal sclerosis), genetic, infectious, metabolic and immune causes; often unknown.
guidelines: ILAE operational classification of seizure types (2017)
diseases.cure: Most people become seizure-free on medication; surgery can cure selected drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy.

pathway.txt: Classify the seizure type (focal or generalised) and look for a cause.

diseases.name: Migraine
diseases.intro: Migraine is a common primary headache disorder with recurrent attacks of throbbing headache, often with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound; about a third of people have aura. The trigeminovascular system and the messenger CGRP are central to attacks.
causes: A largely genetic brain disorder; attacks involve activation of the trigeminovascular system with release of CGRP.
related: frequent use of acute drugs can make headaches more frequent
guidelines: European Headache Federation guideline on anti-CGRP antibodies (2022)
diseases.cure: Not curable; acute and preventive treatments reduce attacks.

pathway.txt: Established acute treatments (for example NSAIDs and triptans); the 2021 consensus found no evidence to change these principles.

diseases.name: Huntington's disease
diseases.intro: Huntington's disease is an inherited, autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disease caused by an expanded CAG repeat in the HTT gene. It causes chorea and other movement problems, cognitive decline and psychiatric symptoms, typically starting in adult life.
causes: Expanded CAG repeat in HTT; longer repeats tend to cause earlier onset. The abnormal huntingtin protein damages neurons, first in the striatum.
related: for example drug-induced or autoimmune chorea
guidelines: Huntington disease primer (Nature Reviews Disease Primers, 2015)
diseases.cure: Not curable; no disease-modifying therapy yet. Huntingtin-lowering drugs are in trials.

pathway.txt: Genetic test for the HTT CAG repeat, with genetic counselling.
A VMAT2 inhibitor (tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine or valbenazine) reduces dopamine release; valbenazine improved chorea in a phase 3 trial.

diseases.name: Frontotemporal dementia (behavioural variant)
diseases.intro: Behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia is a degeneration of the frontal and anterior temporal lobes that usually begins before 65. It changes personality and behaviour: disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive behaviour, changed eating, and executive problems.
causes: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration; a sizeable minority of cases are inherited (for example C9orf72, MAPT, GRN).
related: FTD and ALS overlap clinically and genetically (C9orf72)
guidelines: International consensus criteria for behavioural-variant FTD (2011)
diseases.cure: Not curable; no approved drug changes its course.

pathway.txt: Consensus criteria: at least three of disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive behaviour, changed eating and executive problems; supported by frontal and/or anterior temporal atrophy on imaging.
No drug changes the course; care focuses on safety, support for families and carers, and treating distressing symptoms.

diseases.name: Dementia with Lewy bodies
diseases.intro: Dementia with Lewy bodies is a common dementia caused by alpha-synuclein (Lewy body) pathology in the cortex. Typical features are fluctuating attention, well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and parkinsonism.
causes: Alpha-synuclein aggregation (Lewy bodies), often with Alzheimer-type changes as well.
related: the same protein; dementia in Parkinson's disease is closely related
guidelines: Fourth consensus report of the DLB Consortium (2017)
diseases.cure: Not curable; treatment is symptomatic and largely based on expert opinion.

diseases.name: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
diseases.intro: Obsessive-compulsive disorder causes intrusive, distressing thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviours or mental acts (compulsions) that the person feels driven to perform. It often starts in childhood or adolescence.
causes: Genetic and environmental factors; altered activity in loops between the orbitofrontal cortex, striatum and thalamus.
guidelines: Meta-analysis of treatments in children and youth (2024)
diseases.cure: Often a long-term condition, but many people improve greatly with therapy and medication.

pathway.txt: Exposure and response prevention (a form of CBT), alone or combined with an SSRI; ERP alone or with an SSRI is probably more effective than an SSRI alone (children and youth).

diseases.name: Post-traumatic stress disorder
diseases.intro: Post-traumatic stress disorder can follow a traumatic event: the person re-experiences it in intrusive memories and nightmares, avoids reminders, and stays on high alert.
causes: Trauma exposure together with individual vulnerability; fear memories stay overly active.
diseases.cure: Many people recover with trauma-focused therapy.

pathway.txt: Trauma-focused psychological therapy: trauma-focused CBT has the largest evidence base; EMDR is also effective. Multicomponent approaches work best after complex trauma.

diseases.name: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
diseases.intro: ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition with persistent inattention and/or hyperactivity and impulsivity that start in childhood and affect daily life; it often continues into adulthood.
causes: Highly heritable; many genes of small effect plus early environmental factors.
diseases.cure: A lifelong difference for many; treatment improves symptoms and functioning.

diseases.name: Tourette syndrome and tic disorders
diseases.intro: Tourette syndrome is a neurodevelopmental condition with multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic for more than a year, starting in childhood. Tics often lessen in adulthood; ADHD and OCD frequently co-occur.
causes: Strongly genetic; altered activity in loops between the cortex, basal ganglia and thalamus.
diseases.cure: Tics often improve by adulthood; treatment is for tics that cause distress or impairment.

frontal_pole.note: The very front of the brain. Involved in juggling several goals at once and in thinking about one's own thinking.
frontal_pole.lesion: Subtle problems juggling several goals and planning complex tasks.

sfg.note: Upper strip of the frontal lobe. Supports working memory, attention and self-control of behaviour.
sfg.lesion: Working-memory and planning problems; medial damage near the supplementary motor area reduces self-initiated movement.

mfg.note: The classic 'executive' cortex: holding information in mind, planning and switching strategy. Reduced activity here during working-memory tasks is one of the most replicated findings in schizophrenia.
mfg.lesion: Dysexecutive problems: poor planning, working memory and flexibility. Damage to the frontal eye field here makes the eyes deviate towards the side of the lesion.

broca.n: Inferior frontal gyrus, opercular and triangular parts (Broca's area on the left)
broca.note: On the left side these two parts form classical Broca's area: speech production and grammar. Damage causes halting, effortful speech (Broca's aphasia). The right-side counterpart is involved in stopping actions and in speech melody.
broca.lesion: On the left: non-fluent (Broca's) aphasia with effortful, telegraphic speech and relatively preserved comprehension.

ofc.note: Above the eyes. Weighs rewards and punishments and updates choices when outcomes change. Damage can cause impulsive, socially inappropriate behaviour.
ofc.lesion: Disinhibition, impulsivity and poor social judgement with preserved intelligence.

vmpfc.n: Ventromedial prefrontal cortex (gyrus rectus, medial orbital)
vmpfc.note: Links emotion with decisions and with the value of things to oneself. Part of the cortical midline structures active when we think about ourselves.
vmpfc.lesion: Poor real-life decision-making and changes in emotional behaviour despite normal test intelligence.

mpfc.note: Inner surface of the frontal lobe. Active when we reflect on ourselves and on other people's minds; a core hub of the default mode network.
mpfc.lesion: Apathy and reduced initiative (abulia); reduced reflection on oneself and others.

sca.note: Below the front of the corpus callosum (Brodmann area 25). Regulates mood and bodily stress responses; overactive in depression and a target of experimental deep brain stimulation.

precentral.note: Sends commands to the muscles; the body is mapped upside down along it. Upper motor neurons here degenerate in ALS.
precentral.lesion: Contralateral weakness with upper motor neuron signs; face and hand if the lateral part is damaged, leg if the medial part is damaged.

sma.note: Plans and initiates self-generated movements and sequences. Its activity precedes the conscious feeling of wanting to move; linked to the sense of agency.
sma.lesion: Difficulty starting voluntary movements and speech; sometimes an 'alien hand'.

operculum.note: The 'lid' over the insula. Controls the mouth, tongue and throat for speech and swallowing, and processes taste.
operculum.lesion: Slurred speech and difficulty chewing and swallowing; damage on both sides can abolish voluntary face and tongue movement.

postcentral.note: Receives touch, pain, temperature and position sense from the opposite half of the body, mapped like the motor strip.
postcentral.lesion: Contralateral loss of touch, position sense and the ability to recognise objects by feel (astereognosis).

spl.note: Builds a map of the body and of space for reaching and grasping, combining vision and touch.
spl.lesion: Misreaching for objects under visual guidance (optic ataxia) and problems with body position in space.

smg.note: Part of the inferior parietal lobule. Compares intended with actual movements and helps distinguish self from other; involved in phonological memory.
smg.lesion: On the left: apraxia and conduction-type aphasia; on the right: neglect of the left side of space.

angular.note: Near the temporo-parietal junction. Reading, numbers, meaning, and taking another's perspective; stimulating it has produced out-of-body experiences.
angular.lesion: On the left: Gerstmann syndrome (difficulty writing and calculating, finger agnosia, left-right confusion) and reading problems.

precuneus.note: Inner surface of the parietal lobe. Self-related imagery, memory for one's own life and first-person perspective; a core default mode network hub.

parietal_operculum.note: Processes touch and pain further and integrates them with the insula.
parietal_operculum.lesion: Altered perception of touch and pain.

stg.note: Hears and interprets speech and voices. Abnormal activity here accompanies auditory verbal hallucinations in schizophrenia.
stg.lesion: On the left (posterior part): fluent (Wernicke's) aphasia with poor comprehension; on the right: difficulty understanding the emotional tone of speech.

heschl.n: Transverse temporal gyrus (Heschl's gyrus, primary auditory cortex)
heschl.note: First cortical station for sound, mapped by pitch.
heschl.lesion: Damage on one side causes little loss; damage on both sides causes cortical deafness.

planum_temporale.n: Planum temporale (part of the classical Wernicke's region)
planum_temporale.note: Behind Heschl's gyrus, usually larger on the left. Processes speech sounds. Classical Wernicke's area is a historical, loosely defined region of the left posterior superior temporal cortex that overlaps the planum; damage there causes fluent speech with poor comprehension (Wernicke's aphasia).
planum_temporale.lesion: On the left: poor understanding of speech sounds, part of Wernicke's aphasia.

planum_polare.note: In front of Heschl's gyrus. Processes complex sounds such as music.
planum_polare.lesion: Difficulty perceiving music and complex sounds in some cases.

mtg.note: Word meaning and, at the back, perception of motion and of other people's actions.
mtg.lesion: On the left: difficulty with word meaning; posterior damage can impair seeing motion.

itg.note: End of the 'what' visual pathway: recognising objects and shapes.
itg.lesion: Difficulty recognising objects by sight (visual agnosia).

temporal_pole.note: Tip of the temporal lobe. Knowledge about people and concepts, and social-emotional memory; it degenerates early in semantic dementia.
temporal_pole.lesion: Loss of knowledge about words, objects and people (as in semantic dementia).

fusiform.note: Underside of the temporal lobe. Recognises faces and written words.
fusiform.lesion: Inability to recognise faces (prosopagnosia, right or both sides) or written words (pure alexia, left).

parahippocampal.note: Recognises places and scenes and passes information to the hippocampus.
parahippocampal.lesion: Getting lost in familiar places (topographical disorientation).

entorhinal.note: Main gateway into the hippocampus; contains grid cells for navigation. One of the first areas hit by tau tangles in Alzheimer's disease.
entorhinal.lesion: Memory loss; one of the first areas affected in Alzheimer's disease.

calcarine.note: Receives the visual image from the thalamus; damage causes blindness in part of the visual field.
calcarine.lesion: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often sparing central (macular) vision.

cuneus.note: Above the calcarine fissure; early visual processing of the lower visual field.
cuneus.lesion: Loss of the contralateral lower quarter of the visual field (inferior quadrantanopia).

lingual.note: Below the calcarine fissure; colour and early visual processing of the upper visual field.
lingual.lesion: Loss of the contralateral upper quarter of the visual field; damage on both sides can remove colour vision (achromatopsia).

lateral_occipital.note: Visual areas that assemble edges into shapes and objects.
lateral_occipital.lesion: Difficulty recognising shapes and objects (visual object agnosia).

acc.note: Notices conflict and errors, weighs effort, and links emotion to action. Lesion networks connected to it cause akinetic mutism (loss of the will to act).
acc.lesion: Apathy; damage on both sides can cause akinetic mutism (awake but without spontaneous speech or movement).

mcc.note: Links pain, motivation and the choice of action; connects to the motor system.
mcc.lesion: Reduced unpleasantness of pain (the basis of cingulotomy for intractable pain).

pcc.note: Self-referential thought and autobiographical memory; with the precuneus the main posterior hub of the default mode network. Its metabolism drops early in Alzheimer's disease.
pcc.lesion: Damage to its retrosplenial part causes memory loss and disorientation.

insula_ant.note: Feels the state of the body (heartbeat, breathing, disgust) and turns it into emotion and awareness; core of the salience network.
insula_ant.lesion: Reduced awareness of body signals and disgust; can disturb emotional awareness.

insula_post.note: Receives body signals such as pain, temperature and touch from inside the body.

hippocampus.note: Forms new memories of events and places. Shrinks early in Alzheimer's disease; is smaller on average in schizophrenia.
hippocampus.lesion: Damage on both sides prevents forming new memories of events (anterograde amnesia).

amygdala.note: Detects threat and emotional importance and drives fear learning; linked to anxiety and to the emotional colour of memories.
amygdala.lesion: Reduced fear and difficulty recognising fear in faces; with temporal pole damage on both sides, Kluver-Bucy syndrome.

caudate.note: Part of the striatum. Goal-directed learning and planning; receives dopamine from the substantia nigra. Shrinks early in Huntington's disease.
caudate.lesion: Apathy and reduced spontaneity; its degeneration in Huntington's disease is linked to chorea and cognitive decline.

putamen.note: Part of the striatum. Habitual movements and movement selection; loses its dopamine supply first in Parkinson's disease, which dopamine-transporter scans show.
putamen.lesion: Contralateral movement disorders such as dystonia or parkinsonism; a common site of hypertensive bleeding.

pallidum.note: Has an external (GPe) and an internal (GPi) part; this mesh shows both together. GPi is the main output of the basal ganglia to the thalamus and a deep brain stimulation target in Parkinson's disease and dystonia.
pallidum.lesion: Parkinsonism or dystonia; damage on both sides (for example after carbon monoxide poisoning) causes apathy and parkinsonism.

accumbens.note: Reward, motivation and learning from reward. Receives dopamine from the ventral tegmental area; central to addiction and to the dopamine theory of psychosis.

thalamus.note: Relay and filter for almost all information reaching the cortex, and a hub for attention, sleep and consciousness.
thalamus.lesion: Contralateral sensory loss, sometimes followed by severe pain (thalamic pain syndrome).

ventral_dc.note: Region below the thalamus that in this atlas includes the hypothalamus (hormones, hunger, temperature, sleep) and the upper midbrain nuclei. The substantia nigra, subthalamic nucleus and red nucleus lie in or next to it and are shown separately (MASSP atlas).
ventral_dc.lesion: Hypothalamic damage disturbs body temperature, appetite, sleep and hormones (for example diabetes insipidus).

basal_forebrain.note: Source of most acetylcholine in the cortex, important for attention and memory. Its neurons are lost in Alzheimer's disease, which is why cholinesterase inhibitors are used.
basal_forebrain.lesion: Memory loss with confabulation, for example after rupture of an anterior communicating artery aneurysm.

cerebellum.note: Coordinates and times movements and predicts their sensory consequences; also contributes to thinking and language. Its predictions support the sense of agency.
cerebellum.lesion: Clumsiness on the same side: intention tremor, overshooting (dysmetria) and slurred speech.

vermis.note: Midline of the cerebellum: balance, posture and eye movements; also linked to emotion.
vermis.lesion: Unsteady, wide-based gait and trunk instability (truncal ataxia).

cerebral_wm.note: The wiring of the brain: bundles of insulated nerve fibres that connect cortical areas with each other and with deeper structures. Multiple sclerosis plaques and small-vessel disease damage it.
cerebral_wm.lesion: Depends on the tract: weakness, numbness, visual loss or slowed thinking; scattered lesions occur in multiple sclerosis and small-vessel disease.

cerebellar_wm.note: Fibres entering and leaving the cerebellar cortex, including those of the cerebellar peduncles.

lateral_ventricles.note: Paired fluid-filled cavities where most cerebrospinal fluid is made (choroid plexus). They enlarge in hydrocephalus and when brain tissue shrinks.

third_ventricle.note: Narrow midline cavity between the two halves of the thalamus; connects the lateral ventricles to the fourth ventricle.
third_ventricle.lesion: A blockage here (for example by a colloid cyst) causes obstructive hydrocephalus with headache.

fourth_ventricle.note: Cavity between the brainstem and the cerebellum; cerebrospinal fluid leaves it to surround the brain and spinal cord.

optic_chiasm.note: Where the fibres from the inner (nasal) half of each retina cross to the other side, so each hemisphere sees the opposite visual field. The optic nerve (cranial nerve II) is an outgrowth of the forebrain, not a brainstem nerve: the pathway runs retina, optic nerve, chiasm, optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic radiation, primary visual cortex; a side branch to the midbrain (pretectum and superior colliculus) drives the pupil reflex and eye orienting.
optic_chiasm.lesion: Compression from below (for example by a pituitary tumour) causes loss of both outer visual fields (bitemporal hemianopia).

midbrain.note: Top part of the brainstem. Contains the nuclei of cranial nerves III and IV, the substantia nigra, red nucleus, colliculi and periaqueductal grey, and the cerebral peduncles carrying motor fibres down. In this atlas its front part is included in the ventral diencephalon label. Boundaries approximate.
midbrain.lesion: Weber syndrome (ventral midbrain stroke): third nerve palsy on the same side with weakness of the opposite body.

pons.note: Middle part of the brainstem. Its bulging front (basis pontis) relays the cortex to the cerebellum; its back (tegmentum) holds the nuclei of cranial nerves V to VIII, breathing and sleep centres and the locus coeruleus (noradrenaline). Boundaries approximate.
pons.lesion: Locked-in syndrome after a basilar artery stroke of the front of the pons: paralysis of all four limbs and the face with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements.

medulla.note: Lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord. Holds the nuclei of cranial nerves IX to XII (and parts of V and VIII), centres for breathing, heart rate and blood pressure, the pyramids where most corticospinal fibres cross, and the inferior olive. Boundaries approximate.
medulla.lesion: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome: loss of pain and temperature on the same side of the face and the opposite side of the body, hoarseness and swallowing problems, vertigo, same-side ataxia and Horner syndrome.

sn.note: Dark band in the midbrain whose neurons make dopamine for the striatum (nigrostriatal pathway). Their loss causes the movement symptoms of Parkinson's disease.
sn.lesion: Loss of its dopamine neurons causes parkinsonism on the opposite side.

stn.note: Small lens-shaped nucleus that acts as a brake on movement within the basal ganglia; the most common deep brain stimulation target in Parkinson's disease.
stn.lesion: Wild flinging movements of the opposite limbs (hemiballismus).

vta.note: Midline midbrain dopamine neurons projecting to the nucleus accumbens and prefrontal cortex (mesolimbic and mesocortical pathways), linked to reward, motivation and psychosis.

red_nucleus.note: Midbrain relay between the cerebellum and the motor system; the superior cerebellar peduncle fibres pass through it.
red_nucleus.lesion: With the nearby third-nerve fibres: tremor and ataxia on the opposite side with a third-nerve palsy (Benedikt syndrome).

pag.note: Grey matter around the cerebral aqueduct in the midbrain. Controls pain (the descending pain-inhibition system, a site of opioid action), defensive behaviour (fight, flight, freezing), vocalisation and breathing patterns.

ppn.note: Cholinergic nucleus where the midbrain meets the pons: part of the brainstem locomotor region and of arousal and REM-sleep circuits. It degenerates in Parkinson's disease and progressive supranuclear palsy and has been tried as an experimental stimulation target for freezing of gait.

sup_colliculus.note: Upper pair of bumps on the back of the midbrain (tectum). Turns the eyes and head towards things that appear, using visual input that partly bypasses the visual cortex.
sup_colliculus.lesion: Compression of the upper back of the midbrain (for example by a pineal tumour) causes dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome: loss of upward gaze, pupils that react poorly to light but constrict for near vision, and convergence-retraction nystagmus.

inf_colliculus.note: Lower pair of bumps on the back of the midbrain: the main midbrain relay of the hearing pathway, passing sound information on to the medial geniculate nucleus.

dorsal_raphe.note: Largest group of serotonin neurons, in the midline of the midbrain and upper pons, projecting to the forebrain. SSRIs act on the serotonin these neurons release; adaptation of their autoreceptors is one proposed reason why antidepressants take weeks to work.

median_raphe.note: Midline serotonin neurons in the upper pons, projecting especially to the hippocampus and septum.

habenula.note: Small nucleus above the back of the thalamus that signals worse-than-expected outcomes and suppresses dopamine and serotonin neurons; its overactivity is studied in depression.

lgn.note: Relay in the thalamus for vision: the optic tract ends here and the optic radiation carries the signal on to the primary visual cortex. Each one handles the opposite half of the visual field.
lgn.lesion: Contralateral homonymous visual field loss, sometimes wedge-shaped (sectoranopia).

mgn.note: Relay in the thalamus for hearing: receives from the inferior colliculus and projects through the acoustic radiation to Heschl's gyrus.

claustrum.note: Thin sheet of grey matter between the insula and the putamen, connected with almost the whole cortex. Its function is still debated (attention and salience; a proposed role in consciousness).

internal_capsule.note: Compact band of fibres between the thalamus and caudate on one side and the lentiform nucleus on the other, carrying the motor (corticospinal) and sensory fibres between the cortex and the rest of the nervous system.
internal_capsule.lesion: A small (lacunar) stroke can cause weakness of the opposite face, arm and leg (pure motor stroke), because the fibres are tightly packed.

fornix.note: Arched fibre bundle carrying output from the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies and septal area; part of the Papez memory circuit.
fornix.lesion: Damage on both sides (for example during removal of a colloid cyst) causes anterograde amnesia.

optic_radiation.note: Fibres from the lateral geniculate nucleus fanning back to the primary visual cortex; the lower fibres first loop forward through the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop).
optic_radiation.lesion: Contralateral homonymous visual field loss; damage to Meyer's loop in the temporal lobe causes loss of the upper quarter ('pie in the sky').

acoustic_radiation.note: Fibres from the medial geniculate nucleus to Heschl's gyrus (primary auditory cortex).

corticospinal.note: The main voluntary motor pathway: from the precentral gyrus through the internal capsule, cerebral peduncle, pons and medullary pyramid, where most fibres cross before descending the spinal cord. Its fibres degenerate in ALS.
corticospinal.lesion: Above the pyramidal decussation: weakness with upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, brisk reflexes, extensor plantar response) on the opposite side.

corpus_callosum.note: The largest fibre bundle, connecting the two hemispheres.
corpus_callosum.lesion: Disconnection syndrome: for example, objects felt with the left hand cannot be named when language is in the left hemisphere (after callosotomy or a callosal stroke).

cingulum_bundle.note: Fibre bundle running inside the cingulate gyrus, linking frontal, parietal and medial temporal areas; part of the limbic and memory circuits.

slf.n: Superior longitudinal fasciculus (with the arcuate fasciculus)
slf.note: Long association fibres between frontal and parietal cortex; its arcuate part links the language areas at the front and back of the left hemisphere.
slf.lesion: On the left, damage to its arcuate part is the classic explanation of conduction aphasia (fluent speech and good comprehension but poor repetition).

uncinate.note: Hook-shaped bundle linking the front of the temporal lobe (temporal pole, amygdala) with the orbitofrontal cortex; involved in emotion, social behaviour and naming.

cn3.note: Midbrain, at the level of the superior colliculus, just in front of the aqueduct. Moves the eye up, down and inwards and lifts the eyelid; its Edinger-Westphal part constricts the pupil and focuses the lens (parasympathetic). Schematic position.
cn3.lesion: Third nerve palsy: drooping eyelid and an eye turned down and out; a dilated, unreactive pupil when the parasympathetic fibres are involved.

cn4.note: Lower midbrain, at the level of the inferior colliculus. Its nerve is the only one to leave the back of the brainstem, and it crosses, so each nucleus controls the opposite superior oblique muscle (moves the eye down when it is turned in). Schematic position.
cn4.lesion: Trochlear palsy: vertical double vision, worst when looking down and in (for example on stairs), with a head tilt away from the weak eye; a lesion of the nucleus affects the opposite eye.

cn5.n: Trigeminal motor and main sensory nuclei (V)
cn5.note: Mid pons. The main sensory nucleus handles touch from the face; the motor nucleus drives the chewing muscles. The mesencephalic and spinal trigeminal nuclei extend up and down from here. Schematic position.
cn5.lesion: Numbness of the face on the same side and weak chewing, with the jaw deviating towards the weak side on opening.

sp5.note: Long column from the pons down into the upper spinal cord carrying pain and temperature from the face of the same side; its lowest part (nucleus caudalis) relays head pain in migraine. Schematic position.
sp5.lesion: Loss of pain and temperature sensation on the same side of the face, as in lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.

cn6.note: Lower pons, under the facial colliculus in the floor of the fourth ventricle. Moves the same-side eye outwards and, through the medial longitudinal fasciculus, makes the other eye follow for horizontal gaze. Schematic position.
cn6.lesion: A lesion of the nucleus prevents both eyes from looking towards that side (horizontal gaze palsy), often with a facial palsy because facial nerve fibres loop around it.

cn7.note: Lower pons, in the front-outer part of the tegmentum. Drives the muscles of facial expression on the same side. Schematic position.
cn7.lesion: Weakness of the whole face on the same side, including the forehead (lower motor neuron facial palsy).

vest.note: Floor of the fourth ventricle where the pons meets the medulla: balance, posture and keeping the eyes steady when the head moves (vestibulo-ocular reflex). Schematic position.
vest.lesion: Vertigo, nausea, nystagmus and a tendency to fall towards the side of the lesion.

coch.note: On the outer surface of the brainstem at the junction of pons and medulla: the first relay for hearing, from where sound information travels to both sides. Schematic position.
coch.lesion: Hearing loss in the same-side ear; lesions higher up rarely cause one-sided deafness, because the pathway runs on both sides from here.

nts.note: Medulla, beside the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus: receives taste and signals from the heart, lungs and gut (blood pressure and blood gas sensors). Schematic position.

dmnx.n: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (X)
dmnx.note: Floor of the fourth ventricle in the medulla: parasympathetic control of the heart, airways and gut. One of the first places with Lewy pathology in Parkinson's disease (Braak stage 1). Schematic position.

cn12.note: Medulla, close to the midline under the floor of the fourth ventricle (hypoglossal trigone): moves the tongue. Schematic position.
cn12.lesion: Weakness and wasting of the same half of the tongue, which deviates towards the weak side when stuck out (as in medial medullary syndrome).

amb.note: Front-outer medulla: motor neurons for the muscles of the throat and voice box (swallowing, speech) and parasympathetic neurons that slow the heart. Schematic position.
amb.lesion: Hoarseness and difficulty swallowing, with the uvula pulled away from the side of the lesion, as in lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.

nerve1.note: Olfactory nerve fibres pass through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb, which lies under the frontal lobe; the olfactory tract carries smell back to the brain without a relay in the thalamus. Bulb and tract shown. Schematic course.
nerve1.lesion: Loss of smell on the same side (anosmia), for example after a head injury that shears the olfactory fibres or with an olfactory-groove meningioma.

nerve2.note: Axons of the retinal ganglion cells. An outgrowth of the forebrain rather than a true peripheral nerve. Shown from the optic chiasm to the optic canal (intracranial part). Schematic course.
nerve2.lesion: Loss of vision in that eye with a relative afferent pupillary defect, as in optic neuritis.

optic_tract.note: From the optic chiasm around the cerebral peduncle to the lateral geniculate nucleus; each tract carries the opposite half of the visual field. Schematic course.
optic_tract.lesion: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often incongruous (the two eyes' defects do not match exactly).

nerve3.note: Leaves the midbrain in the interpeduncular fossa, passes between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries, then through the cavernous sinus and the superior orbital fissure. Moves the eye, lifts the eyelid and constricts the pupil. Schematic course.
nerve3.lesion: Ptosis and an eye turned down and out; a dilated pupil when the nerve is compressed, for example by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.

nerve4.note: The only nerve that leaves the back of the brainstem, and the thinnest with the longest intracranial course: around the midbrain, through the cavernous sinus to the superior orbital fissure. Supplies the superior oblique muscle. Schematic course.
nerve4.lesion: Vertical double vision, worst when looking down and in, with a head tilt away from the affected side; often injured by head trauma because of its long course.

nerve5.note: Large root from the side of the pons to the trigeminal ganglion in Meckel's cave, then three divisions: ophthalmic (V1, superior orbital fissure), maxillary (V2, foramen rotundum) and mandibular (V3, foramen ovale). Sensation of the face; chewing muscles. Schematic course.
nerve5.lesion: Numbness of the face on the same side, a lost corneal reflex (afferent limb) and weak chewing; trigeminal neuralgia causes brief electric pains in its territory.

nerve6.note: Leaves the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction near the midline, climbs along the clivus, passes through Dorello's canal and the cavernous sinus to the superior orbital fissure. Supplies the lateral rectus muscle. Schematic course.
nerve6.lesion: The eye cannot move outwards (lateral rectus weakness), with horizontal double vision; a 'false localising sign' when intracranial pressure is raised.

nerve7.note: Leaves the brainstem at the cerebellopontine angle together with nerve VIII and enters the internal acoustic meatus. Muscles of facial expression, taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue, tears and saliva. Schematic course.
nerve7.lesion: Weakness of the whole half of the face including the forehead (as in Bell's palsy), sometimes with loss of taste and sound sensitivity (hyperacusis).

nerve8.note: From the cerebellopontine angle into the internal acoustic meatus: hearing (cochlear part) and balance (vestibular part). Schematic course.
nerve8.lesion: Hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance on the same side, as with a vestibular schwannoma at the cerebellopontine angle.

nerve9.note: Rootlets from the side of the medulla behind the olive, leaving the skull through the jugular foramen. Taste and sensation from the back of the tongue and throat, signals from the carotid sinus, and the parotid gland. Schematic course.
nerve9.lesion: Loss of the sensory limb of the gag reflex and of taste and sensation from the back third of the tongue on the same side.

nerve10.note: Rootlets behind the olive, leaving through the jugular foramen. Muscles of the throat and voice box, parasympathetic supply of the heart, lungs and gut, and sensation from the internal organs. Schematic course.
nerve10.lesion: Hoarseness and difficulty swallowing, with the uvula pulled away from the side of the lesion; damage to its recurrent laryngeal branch paralyses a vocal cord.

nerve11.note: Its spinal root rises from the upper cervical cord through the foramen magnum and leaves with nerves IX and X through the jugular foramen. Supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. The cord part below the template is not drawn. Schematic course.
nerve11.lesion: Weak shoulder shrug (trapezius) and weak turning of the head away from the side of the lesion (sternocleidomastoid).

nerve12.note: Rootlets between the pyramid and the olive, leaving through the hypoglossal canal. Supplies the tongue muscles. Schematic course.
nerve12.lesion: The tongue deviates towards the side of the lesion when stuck out, with wasting and fasciculations.

systems.d: Emotion, motivation and memory: a ring of structures around the brain's core (Papez circuit and its extensions), joined by the fornix and the cingulum bundle. The mammillary bodies belong here but are not separately labelled in this atlas.
Dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra project to the caudate and putamen. Their loss causes Parkinson's disease; D2 blockade by antipsychotics here causes stiffness and tremor.
Cortex to striatum to globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus, back through the thalamus to the cortex: selects and scales movements. The deep brain stimulation targets lie here.

systems.n: Midbrain dopamine pathways to striatum and cortex
systems.d: Dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra project to the striatum and to prefrontal and limbic cortex. In schizophrenia, PET studies find raised presynaptic dopamine mainly in the associative (dorsal) striatum rather than the limbic (ventral) striatum, which argues against the older 'mesolimbic' version of the dopamine hypothesis.

Active when we rest, remember our past, imagine the future or think about ourselves. Its core is the cortical midline (medial prefrontal and posterior cingulate/precuneus); the extended network adds the angular gyrus and medial temporal lobe.

Detects what matters right now, from the body and the world, and switches the brain between inward and outward attention. Defined from brain imaging; core nodes are the anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate.

A proposed functional model, not an anatomical tract: the motor system sends a copy of each command (corollary discharge) so the brain can predict and recognise the result as self-made. Failures are a leading explanation of passivity experiences in schizophrenia.

Plans, starts and coordinates movement: from the motor cortex down the corticospinal tract through the internal capsule and brainstem to the motor neurons of the brainstem and spinal cord (both affected in ALS).

In most people language depends mainly on the left hemisphere: comprehension at the back (posterior superior temporal cortex) and production at the front (Broca's area), joined by the arcuate fasciculus (part of the superior longitudinal fasciculus). Shown on the left side only.
Forms and retrieves memories of events: the hippocampus and its inputs, the fornix, the thalamus and cingulate (Papez circuit). The first system affected in typical Alzheimer's disease.
Keeps goals in mind and controls attention: lateral prefrontal and parietal cortex. Defined from brain imaging.

From the optic nerves and chiasm along the optic tracts (schematic) to the lateral geniculate nucleus, through the optic radiation to the primary visual cortex, then outward to areas for shape, faces, words and motion. A side branch to the superior colliculus turns the eyes towards things.

From the cochlear nuclei through the brainstem to the inferior colliculus and medial geniculate nucleus, then through the acoustic radiation to Heschl's gyrus and the speech and voice areas of the superior temporal cortex.
Nuclei that move the eyes (III, IV, VI) and the structures that coordinate them: vestibular nuclei, superior colliculus, frontal eye field (in the middle frontal gyrus) and cerebellar vermis.

The brainstem nuclei of cranial nerves III to XII (schematic positions). Cranial nerves I (smell) and II (vision) are not brainstem nerves: they grow out of the forebrain. The spinal accessory nucleus (XI) lies in the upper spinal cord, which is not drawn.
Serotonin neurons of the raphe nuclei in the brainstem project to almost the whole forebrain; SSRIs and other antidepressants act on this system.

The twelve pairs of cranial nerves with the optic tract, drawn along schematic intracranial courses from where they leave the brain to the skull base. Use the nerve buttons in the 3D view to show them alone with the brainstem.

systems.n: Cranial nerves with their brainstem nuclei
systems.d: Each nerve in the same colour as its nucleus (schematic), so you can follow a nerve back into the brainstem.

nt.d: The signal of movement, motivation and reward learning: from the midbrain along four classic pathways.

routes.d: Movement selection; these neurons are lost in Parkinson's disease.
Reward, motivation and learning from outcomes.

nt.rec: D1-like (D1, D5) and D2-like (D2, D3, D4) receptors, all G-protein coupled. A fourth pathway, tuberoinfundibular (hypothalamus to pituitary, inhibits prolactin), is not drawn because the pituitary is not in the model.
nt.drugs: Levodopa and dopamine agonists (Parkinson's disease); antipsychotics block D2 receptors; stimulants raise synaptic dopamine.

nt.d: A modulator from the raphe nuclei along the brainstem midline to almost the whole brain: mood, sleep, pain, impulse control.

routes.d: The rostral raphe group projects mainly to the forebrain.
Parallel, overlapping forebrain projections. The caudal raphe group (not drawn) projects to the brainstem and spinal cord.

nt.rec: Seven receptor families (5-HT1 to 5-HT7); 5-HT3 is an ion channel, the others are G-protein coupled.
nt.drugs: SSRIs and SNRIs (depression, anxiety); triptans (5-HT1B/1D agonists, migraine); ondansetron (5-HT3 antagonist, nausea); many atypical antipsychotics block 5-HT2A.

nt.d: Arousal and attention from a tiny nucleus in the rostral pons, the locus coeruleus, to the cortex, thalamus, hippocampus and cerebellum.

routes.d: Widespread forebrain innervation: alertness, attention, stress response.
Cerebellar and spinal projections (spinal cord not in the model).

nt.rec: Alpha-1, alpha-2 and beta (beta-1 to beta-3) adrenergic receptors, all G-protein coupled. The locus coeruleus position is schematic (probabilistic MRI map: Keren et al. 2009).
nt.drugs: SNRIs and atomoxetine block reuptake; clonidine and guanfacine are alpha-2 agonists; beta-blockers act on beta receptors.

nt.d: Attention, learning and memory: from the basal forebrain to the cortex and hippocampus, and from the brainstem to the thalamus.

routes.d: Nucleus basalis: cortical attention and plasticity; degenerates early in Alzheimer's disease.
Septohippocampal projection (septum shown within the basal forebrain label): memory.
Pedunculopontine nucleus: arousal and REM sleep, gait.

nt.rec: Nicotinic receptors (ion channels) and muscarinic receptors M1 to M5 (G-protein coupled). Striatal cholinergic interneurons are local and not drawn.
nt.drugs: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) in Alzheimer's disease; anticholinergic drugs can cause confusion in older people.

nt.d: The main excitatory transmitter: the projection neurons of the cortex, thalamus and hippocampus use it.

routes.d: Voluntary movement; the drawn line ends in the medulla (spinal cord not in the model).
Cortex drives the striatum, the input of the basal ganglia.
The thalamus relays sensation and motor loops to the cortex.

nt.rec: Ion channels (AMPA, NMDA, kainate) and metabotropic receptors (mGluR1 to mGluR8).
nt.drugs: Memantine (NMDA antagonist, Alzheimer's disease); ketamine and esketamine (NMDA antagonists, treatment-resistant depression); riluzole (ALS); perampanel (AMPA antagonist, epilepsy).

nt.d: The main inhibitory transmitter: mostly local interneurons; its long pathways are the outputs of the striatum, pallidum and cerebellar cortex.

routes.n: Striatum to pallidum and substantia nigra
routes.d: Direct and indirect basal ganglia pathways.
The inhibitory output of the basal ganglia.
Purkinje cells inhibit the deep cerebellar nuclei (inside the cerebellar white matter; nuclei not modelled separately).

nt.rec: GABA-A receptors (chloride channels; benzodiazepine site) and GABA-B receptors (G-protein coupled).
nt.drugs: Benzodiazepines and barbiturates enhance GABA-A; baclofen is a GABA-B agonist; several antiseizure drugs act on GABA.

nt.d: A wakefulness signal: all brain histamine neurons sit in the tuberomammillary nucleus of the posterior hypothalamus.

routes.d: Active only during waking; maintains wakefulness and attention.

nt.rec: H1 and H2 (mostly excitatory), H3 (inhibitory autoreceptor and heteroreceptor); H4 mainly outside the brain. Position schematic.
nt.drugs: Sedating antihistamines block H1; pitolisant (H3 inverse agonist) treats narcolepsy; H1 blockade contributes to sedation and weight gain with some psychotropic drugs.

nt.d: A wakefulness stabiliser from the lateral hypothalamus that drives the other arousal nuclei; its loss causes narcolepsy type 1.

routes.d: Keeps the monoamine and cholinergic arousal systems switched on together.

nt.rec: OX1 and OX2 receptors (G-protein coupled). Position schematic.
nt.drugs: Orexin receptor antagonists (suvorexant, lemborexant, daridorexant) treat insomnia.

pathgroups.d: Link the cortex with the deep brain, brainstem and spinal cord.
From the eye to the visual cortex.
The twelve pairs with schematic intracranial courses.

networks.d: Occipital visual areas: from the first analysis of the image to objects and motion.
Moving and feeling the body along the central sulcus; in the Yeo map it also includes auditory cortex.
Goal-directed attention: intraparietal sulcus, frontal eye fields and motion area MT+; selects where to look.
Anterior insula, anterior cingulate and temporoparietal junction: notices what matters and helps switch between networks.
Orbitofrontal cortex and temporal pole. Named 'limbic' in the Yeo map; these areas have weak MRI signal, so it is the least certain network.
Lateral prefrontal and posterior parietal cortex: flexible control, working memory and problem solving.
Medial prefrontal, posterior cingulate and precuneus, angular gyrus and lateral temporal cortex: memory, imagining and thinking about oneself and others.

network_note: Networks from resting-state functional MRI of 1,000 people (Yeo et al. 2011), here from the Schaefer 2018 400-parcel version in the same template space, painted on the 3D cortex (nearest parcel within 4 mm). Networks are statistical groupings of areas that are active together, not anatomical structures; borders differ between people.
